## What The Business Is

Walmart Inc. is a global, people-led and tech-powered omnichannel retailer headquartered in Bentonville, Arkansas, operating retail stores, wholesale clubs, eCommerce websites and mobile apps across the U.S., Africa, Canada, Central America, Chile, China, India and Mexico. Its reportable segments are **Walmart U.S.**, **Walmart International** and **Sam’s Club U.S.**; Walmart describes its purpose as helping customers “save money and live better,” serving about **280 million customers and members weekly** through **10,900+ stores** and digital properties in **19 countries**, with FY2026 revenue of **$713 billion** and about **2.1 million associates**. ([stock.walmart.com](https://stock.walmart.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0000104169-26-000102/wmt-20260430.htm))

## What It Does

Walmart sells grocery, general merchandise, health and wellness items, fuel and other categories through large-format stores, neighborhood formats, Sam’s Club membership warehouses, marketplaces, pickup, delivery and digital channels. In Q1 FY2027, Walmart U.S. net sales were led by grocery at **$70.7 billion**, followed by general merchandise at **$26.4 billion** and health and wellness at **$16.4 billion**; Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales were about **$27.1 billion**, while Sam’s Club U.S. eCommerce sales were about **$4.1 billion**. The company is also building higher-margin adjacent businesses including advertising, marketplace, fulfillment services, membership and data/commerce-media capabilities. ([stock.walmart.com](https://stock.walmart.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0000104169-26-000102/wmt-20260430.htm))

## Recent Highlights (Positive)

Walmart’s Q1 FY2027 results, reported May 21, 2026, showed consolidated revenue of **$177.8 billion**, up **7.3%** year over year, with operating income up **5.0%** and adjusted EPS of **$0.66**; management reiterated FY2027 guidance for constant-currency net sales growth of **3.5%–4.5%**, adjusted operating income growth of **6%–8%**, and adjusted EPS of **$2.75–$2.85**. ([stock.walmart.com](https://stock.walmart.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0000104169-26-000095/0000104169-26-000095.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The transcript highlights continued omnichannel momentum: enterprise eCommerce grew **26%**, Walmart U.S. marketplace net sales grew nearly **50%**, U.S. store-fulfilled delivery more than doubled over two years, and more than **36%** of U.S. store-fulfilled deliveries were completed in under three hours. Management also said Walmart can reach roughly **60% of the U.S. population in 30 minutes or less**, reinforcing the store network as fulfillment infrastructure. ([corporate.walmart.com](https://corporate.walmart.com/content/dam/corporate/documents/newsroom/2026/05/21/walmart-releases-q1-fy27-earnings/q1-fy27-earnings-call-transcript.pdf))

Higher-margin businesses are scaling. In Q1, global advertising grew **37%**, Walmart U.S. advertising grew **36%**, membership fee revenue rose over **17%**, and Walmart later announced a more unified global commerce-media strategy across Walmart Connect U.S., Walmart Connect International and Sam’s Club Connect. ([corporate.walmart.com](https://corporate.walmart.com/content/dam/corporate/documents/newsroom/2026/05/21/walmart-releases-q1-fy27-earnings/q1-fy27-earnings-call-transcript.pdf))

Walmart also extended its speed and value positioning: it announced 30-minute-or-less delivery across **33 U.S. markets**, passed **1 million drone deliveries** across 66 stores in four states and five metro markets, and in early July lowered prices on thousands of seasonal grocery and household items. ([corporate.walmart.com](https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2026/05/28/walmart-brings-30-minute-or-less-delivery-to-33-us-markets))

## Recent Highlights (Negative)

Fuel and consumer pressure were prominent headwinds. Management said Walmart absorbed about **$175 million**, or roughly **250 basis points** of operating-income growth, from higher-than-planned fuel costs in global distribution and fulfillment; executives also noted U.S. consumers were feeling pressure and warned that if elevated costs persist, Walmart would expect somewhat higher retail price inflation in Q2 and the second half of FY2027. ## Bull Case

Walmart's flywheel is compounding: eCommerce up 26%, marketplace up ~50%, advertising up 37%, and membership up 17% — with ads + membership already ~1/3 of operating income. The mix shift toward high-margin, capital-light revenue streams is still early, and general merchandise contributed to gross margin expansion for the first time in 18 quarters. Q2 guidance implies operating income acceleration (7–10% cc) despite a $175M fuel headwind, and supply chain automation (~50% of eComm FC volume automated) sets up a multi-year FCF inflection as the capex wave crests. Share gains from stressed consumers trading down reinforce defensive appeal.

## Bear Case

TTM FCF has declined three straight years ($14.8B → $13.9B → $12.7B) even as revenue grew, meaning the market is paying ~75x EV/FCF and ~39x net income for a mature discounter — a valuation that already fully embeds the ads/marketplace/membership story. Lower-income consumer stress (sub-10-gallon fill-ups), fuel cost absorption, tariff uncertainty, and anniversarying tax-refund and egg-deflation tailwinds all pressure the core. A 7% intraday drop post-earnings shows the stock is priced for perfection; any FCF or guidance disappointment invites sharp de-rating from a 3-year mean market cap of ~$689B.

## Multiple Re-Rating

- **Current implied multiple:** 951,094 / 12,669 = **75.1x EV/FCF**
- **12-month forward multiple:** **63x**
- **Direction:** **CONTRACT**
- **Drivers:**
  1. **FCF normalization mechanically compresses the optical multiple.** Today's 75x is inflated by a capex/automation wave depressing FCF. As FCF recovers toward ~$14.8B, the multiple should contract even with EV roughly flat — the re-rating is largely denominator-driven, not a bearish EV call.
  2. **Catalysts are substantially priced.** The ads/membership/marketplace narrative drove the stock well above its 3-year mean cap; the second derivative of eCommerce growth will slow off large bases, capping further expansion.
  3. **Regime and consumer risk.** Fuel headwinds, low-income consumer stress, and tariff uncertainty argue against paying more per dollar of FCF for a defensive franchise already at premium territory versus history.

## Logic

- Forward FCF: revenue growing ~6–7% cc, automation capex moderating, and mix shift toward ads/membership lift FCF conversion. I forecast FCF recovering to **$14,800M** (roughly back to FY2024 levels, +17% vs. TTM).
- Forward EV = 14,800 × 63 = **$932,400M**.
- EV-to-market-cap bridge: current gap = 951,094 − 887,644 = $63,450M (net debt/leases). Holding the gap constant: forward market cap = 932,400 − 63,450 = **$868,950M**.
- Net result: roughly flat-to-slightly-down market cap (~−2%) — FCF growth is real but offsets an equally real multiple compression as the capex-depressed optics normalize.

Automation (~50% of eComm FC volume) sets up a capex-to-FCF harvest: as the investment wave crests, FCF should inflect well above the depressed TTM $12.7B, driving positive estimate revisions.

## Bear Case
The stock trades at a ~75x EV/FCF optical multiple — much of the ads/membership/automation story is priced. TTM FCF has actually *declined* three years running ($14.8B → $13.9B → $12.7B) as capex absorbs cash. Lower-income consumer stress (sub-10-gallon fill-ups), fuel-cost absorption, tariff/trade uncertainty, and a competitive pricing environment requiring sustained rollback investment all pressure margins. The GM comp benefit may have been juiced by tax refunds and egg deflation traffic that will anniversary. If FCF conversion improves but growth decelerates, the market can de-rate a consumer-staples retailer that has re-rated far above its historical range (market cap ~29% above its 3-year mean).

## Multiple Re-Rating
- **Current implied multiple:** 951,094 / 12,669 ≈ **75.1x EV/FCF**
- **12-month forward multiple:** **62x**
- **Direction:** **CONTRACT**
- **Drivers:**
  1. The current multiple is optically inflated by a capex/automation wave suppressing FCF; as capex moderates and FCF recovers toward ~$15.5B, the optical multiple should mechanically normalize even with a flat-to-modestly-higher EV.
  2. The high-margin mix-shift narrative (ads, membership, marketplace) is now well understood and substantially priced after the multi-year re-rating; incremental upside requires beats, not just delivery.
  3. Maturing top-line (3.5–4.5% cc sales guide) and consumer/fuel/tariff headwinds cap how much premium a defensive retailer can sustain, even as the FCF trajectory improves.

## Logic
1. **Forward FCF:** TTM FCF is $12.7B, depressed by automation/supply-chain capex despite $22.7B net income. With revenue growing ~5–6%, operating income guided +6–8%, and the capex intensity peaking, I forecast 12-month forward FCF of **~$15,500M** (a partial recovery toward the FCF-conversion levels implied by net income, still conservative vs. net income of ~$24B forward).
